Q: State your full name and address for the record.
A: Kelly Bennett, Latham, New York 12110.

Q: Ms. Bennett, my name is Joseph Costyn. I'm an attorney for Ford Harrison. I represent Sterling Planet in the lawsuit you brought against it. Have you ever had your deposition taken before?
A: No.

Q: Okay. The purpose of the deposition is to obtain sworn testimony for the purpose to use in a lawsuit against the company. I will ask a couple of questions that relate to the allegations identified in the complaint and ask you in general about the lawsuit, about your employment with Sterling Planet, and anything that kind of has a relevance to the case. Something that people often do wrong at depositions, they nod or shake their head to give answers. The court reporter can't take that down. So be sure to say yes or no when it's that type of question; give verbal responses.
A: That one won't be a problem for me.

Q: Sometimes the court reporter will get mad if you say um-hum. If you don't understand the question, feel free to interrupt me and ask me to repeat or rephrase the question. That is fine. Sometimes I ask compound questions. I'm not supposed to do that. If there are two questions in one sentence, feel free to stop me and ask me to repeat one at a time. Your attorney will probably do that for you if I do something like that. If anything is unclear, make sure that I know beforehand before you give an answer so we can rephrase the question or state it in a way that you understand it. Is there anything that would prohibit you from giving correct answers today?
A: No.

Q: Have you taken any medication or drugs recently?
A: No.

Q: Is anything present today that could affect your ability to remember past events?
A: No.

Q: In preparation for this deposition, did you review any documents?
A: I reviewed the documentation that Sterling Planet provided through the discovery process.

Q: The documents Sterling Planet has produced, is that correct?
A: Correct. Yes.

Q: Anything else?
A: Whatever I have, whatever we have produced on our end, and whatever you produced on your end.

Q: Documents produced in discovery is what you reviewed in preparation for today?
A: Correct.

Q: Have you reviewed any of the pleadings for the case, like your complaint or any discovery questions or responses that have been given by either party --
A: Yes.

Q: --in preparation for today's deposition?
A: Yes.

Q: What about any notes; have you reviewed notes in preparation for today's deposition?
A: Only notes between attorneys, between myself and my attorney.

Q: Okay. Any tape-recordings or any type of statements that you reviewed?
A: No.

Q: Have you discussed this deposition with anyone other than your attorney in preparation for today's deposition?
A: No.

Q: You have already stated your name. Have you ever been known by any other name?
A: My other name is Kelly Beck, B-E-C-K.

Q: What is your current address?
A: Latham, New York 12110.

Q: How long have you resided there?
A: At least five years.

Q: It's been awhile?
A: It had been awhile.

Q: Do you rent or own?
A: I rent.

Q: What is your current telephone number?
A: 518-782-1931. That's the home number.

Q: You stated you haven't had your deposition taken before, correct?
A: Correct, yes.

Q: Have you ever been involved in a lawsuit before as a plaintiff or as a defendant?
A: No.

Q: This is the first time?
A: Yes.

Q: Let me ask you a couple of questions about your educational background. When did you go to high school?
A: I graduated high school in 1987.

Q: What about college?
A: I almost graduated the first time in 1991 from Binghamton University. I officially got a B.A. from SUNY Albany in ninety -- December '94 I graduated from SUNY Albany.

Q: What did you study?
A: I studied Geography was my major, with Political Science as a minor. And then I got a Master's in Regional Planning from SUNY Albany, and course work at RPI and an MS in Environmental Management Policy.

Q: Outside of college and your educational experience as you have explained to me, have you had any other type of formal training or vocational training, post-college education, anything like that?
A: No, no professional or otherwise.

Q: Do you hold any professional licenses?
A: I do not.

Q: Prior to coining to work for Sterling Planet, what was your job immediately prior?
A: Immediately prior I was Deputy Executive Director for the Environmental Business Association of New York State.

Q: What did you do in that capacity?
A: Everything unofficially. Officially, I was responsible for regulatory policy, for lobbying for policy development. I also did programming for, oh, a hundred plus programs that the organization. I was an interface with our member companies. I was an external interface with other strategic partners, with other associations, and a number of other things. But those were the primarily responsibilities.

Q: Did you have some expertise in the regulatory field that would affect things like clean energy sales and new energy credits?
A: I had a very broad background in environmental policy at that time, which would have included a focus in the energy field. We focused on issues for our members ranging from air to water and everything in between.

Q: All over the place?
A: Yes.

Q: Can you give me a little bit of a description about your environmental policy background? You said you had a broad range of experience.
A: As I described from my education. energy and environmental work has been a core focus of mine from the beginning, from an undergraduate focus even. So I spent my entire career in the environmental and energy field beginning with some work with the State Legislature, working for the Environmental Conservation Committee and working for the speaker staff on environmental and transportation issues primarily there. So it's been what I have done my whole career.

Q: Okay. Have you ever had a job that involved any type of sales or any type -- do you have any type of sales experience prior to your employment with Sterling Planet?
A: I did as early as my freshman year of college when I filled in for my mother who a publisher at a newspaper and had a sales responsibility. I did that for summers. I always was selling. In every job I ever had. I sold. I was external, I was the face of the company, I was an expert in the company. The nature of whatever responsibility I had involved selling. Whether the title said "sales" or "business development" or not, there was always a component of my responsibilities which involved selling. I did that also at Clean Air Technologist, which is a small start-up firm, I did in between the government work and working for the Environmental Business Association. And, you know, I recruited members at EBA, I, I did Member Services at EBA. I sold whatever institution I was working for, for sure.

Q: So whether that be recruiting members or trying to advance the, whatever objective the business had, at the time you considered that to be selling, because you were trying to push a particular agenda for the company, is that right?
A: That's, that's a fair assessment. Sterling Planet was the first company that I worked for that had a product to sell in a traditional definition of selling a product for sales. But, again, everything else was relating to selling a concept, selling an issue, advocating for an issue, selling the benefits of membership in an organization, along those sorts of lines.

Q: Sterling Planet was the first company that had a product that you were in marketing, is that correct?
A: It was, yes.

Q: Talking about the product, we are referring to Renewable Energy Credits, that sort of thing?
A: I also attempted to sell energy efficiency certificates, also known as white tags, and we sold a carbon offset product, as well.

Q: For the record, can you explain what Renewable Energy Credits are?
A: Sure. When you produce renewable energy, you produce two components. You produce an electron, and you produce an environmental attribute called a Renewable Energy Certificate, or a green tag or a green certificate. And it represents the environmental attributes of producing renewable energy and that's a depositive externality.

Q: You mentioned something about white tags. Can you describe what a white tag is?
A: A white tag is one megawatt hour of energy, efficiency of energy not used. And the concept was if you could calculate the environmental benefit of a renewable energy, an electron, you could calculate the benefit of not using a brown energy electron, and so the absence of using dirty energy was clean energy.

Q: The EBA in New York City, what role did someone named Rubinstein play there?
A: Ira Rubenstein was the executive director of the association.

Q: What did he do as executive director?
A: Everything an executive director would do.

Q: Okay. Was he involved in sales?
A: He was certainly involved in member recruitment in the way that I was, in that you were external and in the public eye and were identifying potential members to join the organization and making recommendations to Ed Parker, who was our membership services. We had somebody focused exclusively on membership services, and on selling sponsorships for programs and things like that. So, yes, Ira would have been involved in shaking hands with people in the market, yes.

Q: I think we have had enough background here. One more question about EBA. Did you support Ed Parker?
A: In so much as there were five people, sometimes less, in the office, and Ed had responsibility, again, for raising sponsorship dollars for closing members, oftentimes, we were, we provided leads to Ed. I supported Ed, I supported the front desk, I supported our program person, I supported our energy smart communities person; I supported everybody in the office.

Q: I think we have definitely had enough background here. I want to move on to talk about your employment with Sterling Planet. From the beginning can you describe to me how you first became aware of Sterling Planet and the opportunity to seek employment there? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: Mel Jones was a board members of EBA, and I met him through his function there. As a part of his membership, he provided us some background information on the company. He came to the office with a woman who would eventually become my colleague, Elizabeth Kasprowicz, to talk to our members about a green power option. He came to Albany on occasion for regulatory or other proceedings. There was a renewable portfolio standard proceeding at that time in Albany, and he came here. And I went up the hill and sat with him for awhile and that. So I knew him as primarily as a board member. I was very interested in the company and what the company was doing. I loved the concept, never heard of the concept before. I had been at EBA for awhile and was ready for a change. It was really -- I was really interested in putting my education to practice, which was that corporations were a critical component and I was very interested in getting into the for-profit corporate world.

Q: Did you have any conversations with Mel during his business in Albany as part of the EBA events about potential employment; how did you bring that concept up?
A: I recall I -- that Ed Parker had given me a background on a Green Schools Program that Sterling Planet was thinking of developing, and I loved it. And I called Mel and I said, "I love this. I love this company, how do I get involved? Is there an opportunity for me to get involved." I called him directly on his cell phone -- I called him on his cell phone from my cell phone. And he said, "You would be a great asset, we should talk about it." And I said -- but at that time, it was probably early on and it wasn't an immediate opportunity. It was, do you want to get involved if we can figure out a way for you getting involved. I said. No, I'm interested in employment." Then he said, We need to wait to have a discussion on employment."

Q: Do you remember approximately what date that was when you had the first conversation?
A: I don't recall the exact date, but it would have been in 2005, maybe as early as the summer 2005.

Q: It was several months before you actually started going with the employment process with Sterling Planet?
A: Correct. Yes.

Q: After you had that call with Mel, what happened next as far as your interactions with Sterling Planet about employment?
A: It was, to the best of my recollection, infrequent, other than professional, you know, Mel would come. We perhaps would see each other that way. By the fall of 2005, I was ready to really move. I needed to leave EBA. I hadn't been getting paid. And so it was important for me to take care of myself financially, and my family financially and that was a big motivation. I needed some -- obviously, I needed some consistency there. So I said, "I'm really interested in joining the company, and he said, "Let's see if we can get that done."

Q: You said you were working for EBA, but you weren't receiving compensation?
A: It was sporadic. We were dependent on State funding, and as we know, that can be challenging at best.

Q: I'm aware of that, yes. So you talked to Mel in the fall about moving forward and wanting to work for Sterling Planet, correct, in 2005?
A: Yes, correct.

Q: Chronologically, what happened next in the employment process?
A: Mel sent along an offer letter.

Q: When did you receive the offer letter?
A: It was in December 2005.

Q: Okay. And do you remember approximately when you accepted the employment offer?
A: It was before the end of the year in 2005. I don't recollect what the date of that executed offer letter was and employment contract was, but it, it was before the end of the year, although I didn't start with the company until March of the next year.

Q: When you first started for Sterling Planet, what was your job title?
A: Director, Business Development, Empire Region.

Q: Director of Business Development in the Empire Region?
A: Yes.

Q: Empire referring to New York?
A: New York and New Jersey.

Q: Is that the same job title you had throughout your employment with Sterling Planet?
A: No.

Q: What was the next job title?
A: Director of Northeast Region. That came quickly.

Q: How quickly?
A: Within a couple of months.

Q: Did you maintain the title of Director of the Northeast Region throughout your employment, or did it change again?
A: It changed again to Vice President.

Q: To Vice President? Was there any other title other than Vice President or just --
A: Not initially. In the interim as Director of the Northeast Region, I also assumed, when appropriate, National Policy Director responsibilities, as well -- although it did not ever appear on a business card.

Q: You started out as Director of Business Development for the Empire Region?
A: Correct.

Q: And that changed next to the Northeast?
A: Correct.

Q: After that was Vice President?
A: Correct.

Q: What was the official job title after VP?
A: Then I become VP of Carbon and Efficiency Markets.

Q: What are Carbon and Efficiency Markets?
A: There are - - they were emerging environmental attribute markets. It was a reflection of my role in those markets for the company.

Q: Did you have any other official job title after Vice President of Carbon and Efficiency Markets?
A: No.

Q: As Director of Business Development for the Empire Region, what type of job duties did you have?
A: Sales; I was business development.

Q: How long were you in that role?
A: For the Empire Region role, just two or three months, maybe? I think it was by May of 2006, the title had changed to the Northeast Region.

Q: As Director of Business Development for the Northeast Region, did your job duties change at all, or was it just an expanded territory?
A: It was an expanded territory. It was a broader view. It wasn't exclusive to business development. It also included some regulatory work, as well. So keeping track of what was going on in state houses and the region, interacting with external stakeholders, such as ACORE, or the Environmental Business Association. It was a reflection of a broader scope in a region that was important strategically to the market.

Q: While you were in the business development roles for Empire and for Northeast, what type of products of Sterling Planet were you selling?
A: Primarily Renewable Energy Certificates, REC's. Although as early as 2007, a little before that, maybe towards the end of 2006, I was in discussions with customers around White Tags. There was not a carbon focus in the company and a product line at that point.

Q: What about carbon offsets? Were you involved with carbon offsets at that time?
A: No, minus knowing what they were, minus knowing that they were a product we needed to think about and consider, minus my association with climate leaders, E.P.A. climate leaders, we did not have a specific carbon offset offering. That said, if somebody asked for it, we would have figured it out.

Q: Are renewable credits essentially the same as offsets?
A: No.

Q: What is the difference?
A: The difference is, one, renewable energy, which is a megawatt hour, and the other is the destruction, avoidance of carbon emissions, of a wide range of carbon emissions, greenhouse emissions, really.

Q: During your time doing business development for Empire and for Northeast, were you involved in the sales or the marketing of energy efficiency credits?
A: I don't recall but the first conversation we had with Pfizer -- but that would have been, to the best of my recollection, in 2006, late in 2006, around energy efficiency certificates.

Q: Is that the same thing as White Tags?
A: Correct.

Q: When you moved into the Vice President role, do you know approximately what date that was?
A: It was, it was July 2007.

Q: What brought about that change?
A: I earned it.

Q: What do you mean. Can you give me a little description? I'm assuming it was a promotion, correct?
A: Correct.

Q: Can you explain why you were given the promotion?
A: I was given the promotion, because I was increasingly involved in high profile sales -- including Mohawk Paper -- in regulatory issues, increasingly involved in speaking on a national level on emerging market issues, like energy efficiency certificates and carbon offsets. I was increasingly important from a strategic perspective internally. There was no female vice president. I got to be the first female vice president in the history of the company.

Q: Did you consider yourself to be an expert on the products that Sterling Planet sold and the regulatory affairs, that kind of governed them?
A: As much as one can be in this ever-evolving market.

Q: You said you were speaking on a national basis. Can you tell me about your speaking engagements for Sterling Planet?
A: They arrived by one of two ways. Oftentimes, especially early on, they arrived by Mel Jones calling me oftentimes the night before an event and saying. I'm double booked, I have got an opportunity, can you pinch hit for me? And I would say, absolutely. What are we presenting? But I, I filled in -- much of the national presence was filling in for Mel.

Q: What did you speak about?
A: It depended on the conference. Early on, primarily Renewable Energy Certificates, what is a REC, what is the market, how are they used, what is the difference between voluntary and compliance, the basics, 101.

Q: I understand you're also an expert in regulatory affairs that affected the Renewable Energy Certificate market. Can you describe your expertise in that area to me?
A: I can't explain the expertise in that. I have never written a piece of legislation. I was an expert at knowing how to follow the changes and how to keep abreast of the changes and raising those changes as both challenges potentially and/or opportunities potentially to us from a business perspective and to our customers from a marketing perspective -- was there a risk in the regulatory environment to our customers? Was there an opportunity for us?

Q: How did you track regulatory changes and trends?
A: A number of ways. E-mail, we had membership to a number of professional organizations which provided updates. I had a professional network of people. We were involved in trade associations whose primary responsibility was tracking policy.

Q: Did you receive regular updates from these organizations?
A: Um, on some issues, yes. On some broad issues, I would have to hunt for it. I would have to know where to look.

Q: When you are talking about hunting, how would you go about doing that?
A: Sometimes directly to the regulatory agency's website or a third party who might be tracking legislation, or an NYSERDA-like entity who has very broad focus.

Q: Did you ever participate in letters, comment on rule making?
A: I did, yes.

Q: Did you ever publish any comments?
A: We did publish comments. I recall specifically in Connecticut with the Connecticut DPUC. And I may have done other comments. By the time we were very much involved in rule making and regulatory comments, we were involved in an association called REMA, R-E-M-A, Renewable Energy Marketer's Association, which was writing a lot of the substantive work on behalf of the organization. There were other activities that took place that others may have been involved with, too.

Q: You mentioned the DPUC. What does the DPUC stand for?
A: The Department of Public Utilities Commission, or Public Utility Commission.

Q: So that was your involvement with the rulemaking of the Connecticut DPUC -- at the state level, not at the national level?
A: Correct. I don't recall that we ever submitted any comments in any federal proceeding.

Q: In addition to your knowledge of the regulatory development in the industry, what other type of steps did you take to keep yourself informed about developments in the renewable energy market, in general?
A: I read voraciously, I attended numerous conferences, I had conversations with customers, with colleagues, with external parties. I asked my colleagues, including Mel, including Marcus Krembs, including anybody else -- Bob Maddox was a great resource to me. I had a steep learning curve initially, and after -- you know, it was a small market. If you needed to get educated, you could find out how to get educated. If you didn't know something and it didn't exist, it meant that maybe there was an opportunity to create it.

Q: Did Sterling Planet ask you to, or rely on you, to inform its customers about regulatory changes or regulatory affairs in the industry?
A: On occasion, when required.

Q: How did your knowledge of the regulatory issues that affected Renewable Energy Credits and the market in general add value to your job? How did you use that in your employment with Sterling Planet?
A: We existed because of a regulatory environment. Many of our customers, not all, created products and services because of a regulatory policy environment, whether it was a voluntary policy or whether it was a mandatory policy. So having knowledge around the drivers for decision-making, both from a compliance perspective, why a utility would need to buy a Renewable Energy Certificate under a mandate, or whether it was why Intel wanted to buy a Renewable Energy Certificate voluntarily. So it was a key component of the drivers of purchasing, both from, either from a mandatory perspective or voluntary perspective.

Q: In your sales activities that you described earlier, did you continue to do that as a Vice President?
A: I did.

Q: In your VP program for carbon and efficiency markets, did your duties change at all to go along with the times? Were you involved with carbon efficiency markets in a different way than you were before?
A: The -- my -- I will take the first part of the question first. My responsibilities. my responsibilities did not fundamentally change. The external focus was what was meant to change. It was meant to signal a high level acknowledgment, expertise at Sterling Planet to the external market. It was as much an external communication as it was an internal communication. That said, the management of our carbon focus and our efficiency focus internally was disparate. Was this a supply issue, was this a project issue? Was it a sales issue? Who was the person who would make that decision? Who would review where we got our supply? Who would review what our price was for our product? That was not handled necessarily in one place. So it was meant in that change to aline myself and Marcus Krembs, who for, I think, most of his tenure had title of Director of Greenhouse Gas Programs or something along those lines. So it was meant to have an internal "go-to" team. We were to work directly with Mel. We were to handle -- Marcus was the supply side and I was the coordination of the sales side, and, of course, there was always the what's going on in the regulatory market and/or the voluntary market for that matter.

Q: Did this carbon efficiency market, did that refer to carbon offsets into white tags?
A: Broadly, yes.

Q: Was there any other product the company sold in the carbon or efficiency markets other than carbon offsets or white tags?
A: Could you repeat that? Sorry.

Q: Were there any other products that the company sold within what we call the carbon efficiently markets, other than carbon offsets or white tags?
A: You could sell a REC to anybody under any circumstances. A REC could be used for customers focused on carbon. That person, that customer, could buy REC's to meet a carbon reduction goal, a greenhouse gas reduction goal. So even though it said carbon and efficiency certificate, REC's, were still the primarily driver for customers in dealing with carbon. It was, it was more a reflection of the evolution of the market from a pure REC green power driver to a carbon reduction or carbon management driver, and REC's were a very important part of carbon efficiency from that perspective.

Q: Earlier you mentioned Marcus Krembs. Can you tell me who he was?
A: Marcus was the Director of Greenhouse Gas Programs. My association with him -- I believe that was his title. Early on, he may have had a different title, I don't recall what that was. He was on the supply side of the house.

Q: What do you mean by the supply side?
A: We were bifurcated. So we had a sales side and we had a supply side. Those people that sold REC's and those people who delivered on the contracts, who bought the REC's.

Q: Where did people on Marcus's, on the supply side, where did you they purchase REC's from?
A: Hundreds, potentially, of suppliers.

Q: Were the suppliers, did they originate the renewable energy credits, or were they middlemen or resellers of credits?
A: Could you clarify that? Who was the originator, was Marcus the originator of the REC's?

Q: The hundreds of potential sources that you're describing that Sterling Planet would purchase renewable credits from, were they originators of these credits, or were they resellers?
A: The supply team worked with both brokers in the market, who would have been middlemen, and the supply team also worked with the renewable energy generators, with owners of renewable energy assets.

Q: For the record, can you describe how the Renewable Energy Credits are originated or created in the first place?
A: It depends on the rule, but in the basic sense when you have a renewable energy project defined by a particular body, regulatory or voluntary, you create renewable energy. If -- it may depend on when that project was, when it came online, when the switch was flipped. It may be that the switch could have been flipped, but they weren't eligible to sell into a market until 10 years later. It all depended on the rules and all depended on the definition and all depended on the buyer's preference, as well.

Q: Going back to Marcus, did you ever supervise him, or did he ever report to you?
A: He did from about -- for a very short period of time, apparently. I believe the title change for me came in October of '08 -- maybe it was earlier than that.

Q: Which title?
A: To the carbon efficiency markets. To specify, VP of Carbon and Efficiency Markets. That is when Mel made the decision to have Marcus come and sit in that group, and that group was me and Marcus with Marcus reporting to me.

Q: Marcus Krembs started reporting to you around October '08?
A: To the best of my recollection. There is an e-mail that I wrote for Mel to announce the change that I sent to him that he approved, but was never sent out. So whether that was official that Marcus report to me or not, it was certainly never broadcast to anybody else in the company.

Q: The e-mail you are referring to, is that a document that has been either produced by either party in the discovery of this case?
A: It has, yes.

Q: Was that provided by Sterling Planet for you?

A: I don't, I don't think I sent an e-mail about my commissions.

Q: Is there any reason why you did not make a request, written or oral, to be paid commissions while working for Sterling Planet? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: Did you ask me the reason that I didn't?

Q: Yes.
A: There were -- the primary reason was the process I just described. There was a lag in a sale versus purchasing supply and knowing net profit for that supply. I also had a number of negative interactions with the CFO around pricing. And I was told, for example, that one of my contracts was -- we are going to lose money on the contract. I wasn't on the supply side, didn't know about pricing. I didn't know if he was right or wrong, but I certainly wasn't going to make a demand for payment of something that my CFO was telling me was under water.

Q: Who was the CFO you are referring to?
A: Robert Purser.

Q: Do you remember the specific transaction that you just described that was under water?
A: It was the Mohawk Paper contract.

Q: By "under water" do you mean Mr. Purser indicated the supply costs exceeded the sales price of the contract?
A: That's correct. And his concern was driven by the new sales price in the contract that I renegotiated, which was a decrease in approximately two dollars a REC. He was very concerned about supply costs. My response to him was you will be able to make it up in volume, and I will be the only one hurt because I wouldn't be able to get commission on it, I guess, then.

Q: When you said make it up on volume? What does that mean?
A: It means that that sale was a hundred thousand REC's. You were going to sell a million REC's that year or five million REC's. If you lost on 100,000, you had a chance to make it up on the other 900,000. And shortly after that, we changed our prices and increased our prices. You will see that reflected in my spreadsheet.

Q: During the time you were employed by Sterling planet, were any of the agents who did sales for the company paid any commi s s ions ?
A: I knew that Allan Zox had been paid commissions, I knew that Charles Segerman had been paid commissions, I knew that Bill Bastuk and Gary Skulnik and John Me Keller were asking for commissions, and they were ultimately paid some commission.

Q: Did you ever take any action to insure that an agent was paid their commission?
A: Yes.

Q: What action was that?
A: For Charles Segerman I went through every Quickbase record, went back to the sales contracts, utilized Mel's Excel spreadsheet, did not have an End-User Referral Form. There was no End-User Referral Forms on any of the sales that Charles Segerman executed. And I checked with accounts payable to see whether we had received payment from those customers on those sales and relied on Mel to provide to me that supply cost to calculate Charles's net profit and commission. And I did the same. except that I didn't have the benefit of the original Excel spreadsheet from Mel for -- and it wasn't as complex -- for Gary Skulnik and Bill Bastuk, and John Me Gregor -- I'm sorry Me Keller. They had just a couple of sales. But I, I went to Quickbase, I made sure the record was in Quickbase, I made sure it was closed. I printed those records, and attached it with an Excel spreadsheet modeled after the one Mel had created for Charles for each of the three of them that I submitted to Accounts Payable with a check request form so they could be get paid.

Q: Why did you did take those actions to help them get paid?
A: They had followed the required process for agents, which was the Quickbase account and records and payment by the customer. And then we had to figure out how to deal with supply costs. That was not a known cost sometimes, and that was a problem.

Q: How was supply cost not a known cost?
A: As I described the supply for the sales for Charles's, as well, may not have been purchased, or if it had, it might not have been known. I couldn't match up that electron from that product -- um, project with that particular sale. So Rob Henry, in this example, had, in essence, just created an place holder value, an average that he felt comfortable with using. MR. COSTYN: All right. I will show you what has been previously marked as Plaintiff's Deposition Exhibit 6. For the record, this is a document that was provided in DISCOVERY. Like the last exhibit, it does not have a Bates stamp number on this copy, however, after the deposition, I will provide that to counsel. BY MR. COSTYN:

Q: Ms. Bennett, do you recognize this document?
A: I do recall this discussion about Bill and Gary with Vai. It reflects in writing the process that I just described. That is page one and two. I don't know who Kelly Keswick is at the top of this page. I don't recognize that name from any of the documents that you have provided so I, I may have -- so that's an issue. And the attachment, the Agent Commission appears to be that Excel spreadsheet that I just described that Mel had created that I used to calculate commissions for Bill with Larsen and Navalis, your page four, which I don't ever recall seeing in your discovery documents. But it -- I was asked at one point to create a list of known agents. This may be that list. I don't remember you providing this to us, however.

Q: Were there any other written communications that you engaged in with the company to insure an agent or anyone else was paid commissions as owed to them? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to the form.
A: There were, there were similar discussions with a single sale, I believe, that John Me Keller closed. Then there are multiple e-mails between Mel and me and Gary Skulnik and Charles Segerman regarding his commissions.

Q: You say that was Segerman and Skulnik?
A: Yes.

Q: While you were a Vice President in Sterling Planet, did any agents report directly to you?
A: I managed the agent's program.

Q: Can you describe what you did in that role?
A: I sent out a contract to them, I made sure the contract came back in, I trained them. If they needed training on the basics of the industry, I trained them on the specific products and services that we offered. I trained them on Quickbase. I explained to them the importance of Quickbase. I assisted them with customers. I went on, for example, the sales calls with Bill Bastuk with Larsen and Navalis, met with them. I was troubleshooting for them, took their complaints and ultimately congratulated them when they closed a sale and facilitated their commission payment.

Q: During the time you were employed, did you ever take any action to calculate or estimate commission that you thought was owed to you? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I had a ballpark figure in my head not knowing what a supply cost could be, not knowing what the net profit might be and what I thought I earned from a commission perspective.

Q: Did you have anything in writing to calculate your commissions and what was due to you?
A: I had Quickbase. That is all in my view that I needed, and I had executed sales contracts.

Q: In Quickbase the assistance you referred to, does it have an input field or -- I'm trying to think how to describe this -- any type of field that has the word "commission" in it where it contains commission percentages for a particular sale?
A: It does not have a commission field nor does it have a supply price field.

Q: Did you ever take any action to determine what the specifics of supply costs were for any transactions for which you are currently claiming to be entitled to commi s s ions ?
A: I did not take action to get the final supply costs. Again, I knew from senior management what the general overall profit margin was, so I could in my head estimate and, when appropriate, have the real number to put in there. That real number was not something I controlled, that I had access to, not on the company drive, not in my job duties. I had no access to supply contracts. I had no supply contracts in my possession.

Q: Did you ever request supply contract pricing information in order to determine the amount of commissions due to any of the agents that you is supervised?
A: I did not go to a single supply contract. I did not have access to supply contracts. I had access to the manager of supply who had access to that information. And when I needed that number in your exhibit 6, page three, and the agent commission spreadsheet, the unit cost of REC's in that column was provided to me by Rob Henry based on a calculations known only -- well, I don't know only to him, but to him and not to me.

Q: So whenever you needed to obtain contract information, you would contact Rob Henry?
A: Or whomever. At this point it was Rob Henry. Prior to this point, it could have been Ron Mitchell, could have been Joe Barclay. It could always be determined, theoretically, so long as you had the supply purchase, so long as somebody was willing to give you that number.

Q: When you requested supply contract information from Rob Henry or Ron Mitchell or Joe Barclay, in what format would it have been provided to you or was it provided to you? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I would have generally phoned them and asked them for that information. I might have sent an e-mail to Ron or to Joe or to Rob, or to Mel, perhaps. That information would have been provided to me, either verbally or in writing, or they could have filled out the spreadsheet. We had a verbal conversation about the specifics of this, of the agent coirunissions, those few that were paid by me, via me was a broad conversation around agents in general and how were we going to do this.

Q: It was not a specific procedure for information that was used?
A: It was ad hoc.

Q: You got the information ad hoc?
A: Yes.

Q: Okay. Are you aware whether supply contract information would have been available for any of the sales to which you claim entitlement to a commission while you were employed? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to the form.
A: If I had a sale in reporting year 2008 and it was a Green-e sale, then by Green-e rules that supply would have to be purchased by March of 2009. So if we follow the Green-e rules, then that supply for the Green-e sale would have to be purchased by that particular point. That was my understanding of the process. I can't tell you for certain at any point whether or nor the supply was purchased. whether generator attestations were delivered for the supply contracts.

Q: You mentioned Green-e. What is Green-e.
A: Green-e is the Center for Resource Solutions, and it's a watch dog entity in the green power market for voluntary purchases.

Q: Is it a governmental agency or a nonprofit organization?
A: It's a -- I think it's a nonprofit organization, non-governmental.

Q: What do you mean by watch dog?
A: They publish rules for both a generator and a wholesaler, for Renewable Energy Certificates, that if you want to order a Green-e REC, you follow their rules, and there are open transparent rules where anyone can see whether you are a participant in the market or not. And they have a fairly rigorous auditing process to preserve the integrity of the transactions in the voluntary market.

Q: Do you ever sell any Renewable Energy Credits to any of the customers that are listed on this exhibit, entities to which you were claiming commission you are entitled to? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to the form. Sorry. Did you ever sell REC's that were not Green-e?
A: The utility programs do not have a Green-e requirement. They have their own requirements. To the best of my knowledge, without looking at every single sales contract in detail, those companies that I'm claiming commissions for sales I'm claiming commissions for, otherwise should be Green-e sales.

Q: How would a sale be certified as Green-e?
A: It's paper. It's what we propose and a pricing table, and it's what the customer specifies and it's what's in the contract.

Q: What's your understanding of Green-e rules regarding when supply for a particular sale has to be purchased?
A: If you are buying and report in the reporting year 2010, your supply can be purchased from June, July 1st until July 1st, 2009 through March 31st, 2011. You need to bring a REC generated during that time period to fulfill that reporting year contract. Those were the rules as I understood them as of July 15th, 2009 when I left employment with Sterling Planet.

Q: To borrow on energy credits for a certain reporting year according to the Green-e, it's permissible to purchase REC's that are generated during that year, not necessarily during that year but during a window that could fall during several months of the previous year and several months of the next year; is that correct?
A: That's correct.

Q: Do you know how many months to buy REC's they were generated, that were generated in the preceding year?
A: I'm not sure I understand the question.

Q: I'm not sure I understand my question, either. If you were to buy REC's for 2010, in that year how many REC's back in 2009 could you have generated during that time? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to the form. My understanding -- again, I will make a disclaimer, this is not my side of the house.
A: Yes. My understanding in reading and knowing what I know of the Green-e rules, the eligibility for delivery for a reporting year for a 2010 contract would be that Rob Henry could buy a REC that was generated from an eligible facility from July 1st, 2009 until March 31st, 2011. So you could go back six months, you can buy anything that year that you purchased. Then you can go forward the next month. Oftentimes you had big purchases at the end of a reporting year and also have big supply purchases in March and all of your supply for 2009 would need to be purchased by March of 2010.

Q: You would go back six months and forward three months basically outside of the actual reporting year with the rest being supplied to you? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to the form.
A: If I, if I wanted a reporting year 2010 REC's, Green-e eligible 2010 REC, I could go back six months and could go forward three from that reporting area. That is my unders tending.

Q: I think I get it now. Going back to the spreadsheet that you provided to Sterling Planet along with your demand letter, which I believe was Exhibit 1 -- sorry, I believe it's Exhibit 3 -- the column that's headed up as Contract Date, what do those dates represent?
A: That is the date that the contract was executed.

Q: Where did you obtain the information to populate that column?
A: That information came from Quickbase.

Q: Who would have entered that in Quickbase?
A: I would enter contract information, sales information from my customers in Quickbase. Oftentimes, Valerie Christopher, the Contract Administrator, would be the last person to check that record to make sure that the Quickbase record when it was closed matched the final contract. She was the last person to put her hands on a contract. And the last thing she did was check Quickbase; it's on the checklist.

Q: The column that's entitled Contract Term, what do those numbers represent?
A: That represents how many years that, the number of years for the contract.

Q: Was that information obtained from Quickbase as well?
A: That information comes from Quickbase put in by the sales rep who manages their customers in Quickbase and confirms when it's closed by the contract's administrator.

Q: Tell me about the end of your employment with Sterling Planet. MR. WALLENDER: Objection to the form. On what date did your employment with Sterling Planet officially terminate?
A: July 15th, 2009.

Q: Were you terminated or did you resign?
A: I was terminated.

Q: What was the stated reason for your termination?
A: The stated reason was my refusal to relocate to the corporate headquarters in Atlanta.

Q: Were you requested to relocate to the corporate headquarters by Sterling Planet?
A: It was never in any written document ever formally requested or demanded that I relocate to Sterling Planet. I had numerous conversations about how valuable I would be to the company if I was in the Atlanta office all the time. Mel's position was it was completely unnecessary, because I was so externally focused.

Q: You are saying it was Mel's position that your presence would not be required in your office?
A: Verbally he stated that to me multiple times.

Q: Who at Sterling Planet orally requested you to move to Atlanta? MR. WALLENDER: Object to form.
A: Sonny Murphy had a conversation with me in December of '08 that he was seriously considering having folks come, external folks, come down and be in Atlanta. They were having a hard time managing external people. His -- and his view was that would be an appropriate and necessary step to take, to consolidate.

Q: Was there anyone other than Sonny Murphy who you had a discussion with about moving to Atlanta? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I had multiple conversations about relocation with Mel, none of which required me -- none of which included his demand that I relocate.

Q: What was the substance of his conversations?
A: "It would be great to have you here," "You know, you are always welcome here. Your family comes first. We didn't hire you to be in Atlanta. You are doing a great job out there."

Q: It is it correct these conversations occurred towards the ends 2008? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: Specify which conversations.

Q: The conversations with Sonny and Mel about possibly relocating?
A: The conversations about, "Boy, wouldn't it be great," happened fairly near to my hire, within the first year, say, because I was adding a lot of value. Those were early on and not frequent, but occasional. The conversation with Sonny -- there was a conversation with Sonny in December '08 and it was not -- it was "We really would like you to think seriously about this. You can have a job or you can have a career."

Q: What was your response to Mr. Murphy?
A: My response was that because of my family situation, that it prohibited me from relocating to Atlanta. I was separated, I could not move my only child 1500 miles away from her father.

Q: Are you and your husband still separated?
A: Are we still? Yes.

Q: Was there a formal divorce?
A: There is not a formal divorce in place. We have been legally separated.

Q: Have there been any legal proceedings that have been related to the separation? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to form.
A: We have a legal separation.

Q: At any time did you ever have to fill out a financial affidavit or any other type of document describing your income and assets as part of that separation?
A: I don't recall what we filled out in the separation document. I don't recall what kind of financial information I had to fill out. It was very amicable. I said I owe you nothing, he owes me nothing, that's it. I honestly don't recall. I don't have a lot of assets. It's not a big part of the proceeding.

Q: In the lawsuit you contend Sterling Planet breached a contract with you, you have been damaged by that breach by Sterling Planet not paying the commission. Is the contract that is referred to, there is an offer letter that is Exhibit 1 in today's deposition? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I don't know what document you're referring to. Can I see a copy?

Q: Exhibit 1.
A: You referred to another --

Q: The Complaint. The Complaint in paragraph one.
A: I need to see it to make sure I'm answering truthfully. MR. COSTYN: Can I hand her copy of this? I believe this is a the copy of the Complaint. Do you have a copy? MR. WALLENDER: You were showing me the Complaint that was an Amended Verified Complaint?

Q: You allege that Sterling Planet breached the contract with you by its failure to pay you commissions; is that correct?
A: Yes.

Q: The contract that you allege had been breached by Sterling Planet; is that the offer letter that you signed that is Exhibit 1 in today's deposition? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: Yes.

Q: Also in your lawsuit, you claim Sterling Planet failed to provide you with shares of stock, referring to the Plaintiff's 1; is that where you claim your stock claim?
A: Yes, stocks are paragraph four and commissions are paragraph five.

Q: Are there any stock options that you contend have been breached by Sterling Planet?
A: Unless specified in a Complaint somewhere, none that I can think of, commissions and stock.

Q: Also in your lawsuit you allege that Sterling Planet breached a duty of good faith in fair dealing. On what facts do you base that claim?
A: I'm not sure that I know the legal definition of that. Can you define those terms for me?

Q: Well, you allege in the lawsuit --
A: I'm not a lawyer.

Q: I understand -- that Sterling Planet breached a duty to act in good faith and deal with you fairly. On what facts do you base that claim? How did it breach the duty of good faith in dealing to you? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I had a contract. I had an employment agreement with certain terms and conditions that I had a reasonable expectation that I would be compensated. I was on every element that I had the ability to control, whether it was salary or commission -- or bonuses, rather, I had good faith after multiple conversations with the senior most level of the company, that I had stock, that I was building value, personal wealth in terms of commissions, and corporate wealth, which was the most important thing to me. And when I was terminated and when I asked for the first time in a formal way, it never had an employment review, couldn't ask for things formally, they didn't have the process. When I finally had the process through my termination of asking for it, those terms and conditions were not met.

Q: Are there any other facts on which you base your claim for the breach of good faith in fair dealing? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I think, I think I've laid out the most relevant facts in our document and here today. We had a system and a process, and I filled out -- I, I met those conditions.

Q: When was the first time that you made a request to Sterling Planet to be paid commi s s ions ? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: If you're referring to -- could you clarify?

Q: Okay. Your first oral or written request to Sterling Planet to be paid commissions that you felt you were owed? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I had a direct conversation with Sonny. I had a follow-up conversation with Rob Henry, who was acting as the HR rep for Sterling Planet during my separation process.

Q: Do you recall when your conversation with Sonny Murphy occurred?
A: Well, I made a demand in writing for commissions and for stock. I'm not sure whether that was prior to my departure or after. I had a verbal conversation with him. In one of the conversations that took place between May 22nd, which was the original phone call from Mel, to the last conversation I would have had with Rob Henry, was post termination date. So it would have been, there was conversations with Sonny before I was fired, there were conversations with Rob Henry after my last day. I don't recall the date of that conversation. It was -- It was an overwhelmingly administrative discussion regarding sick time, commissions, stock options, what do I do with my computer.

Q: Are you referring to a letter that you wrote to Sonny, that is exhibit 3, as to your position?
A: That was a part of it. That was the first time, I believe, I -- it was in response to a voicemail that I had left to, with Rob Henry asking, again, about what he learned about commissions and stock and vacation and sick, if any. And Sonny sent a letter and asked for -- and I mentioned on that voicemail that I had documentation -- and Sonny asked for it, and this was the response to Sonny.

Q: Did Sonny call you back after you left the message with Rob?
A: Sonny sent -- Sonny did call me after I left the voicemail for Rob Henry. I remember it was late on a Friday and I didn't get it. And he mentioned on the voicemail that he was with Martha Ann in Florida, and that he'd get back to me on it, that Rob had been out of the office, he would get back to me on it. And there's a letter after this, that is they will get back to me on it, which was, as you know, "not entitled". His position was the company never paid commissions.

Q: Did you engage in any other written communication Sterling Planet regarding your commi s s ions ? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form. Regarding your claim for commissions?
A: The written communication is what we've covered here.

Q: When did you first -- sorry, I'll rephrase that. When did you decide to file a lawsuit against Sterling Planet?
A: When I asked -- upon, before being terminated, and in the process of being terminated -- about commissions and about stock, and my answer was that I was not entitled to them, that the company had never paid commissions, and that I had no stock, there was no stock to anybody, that I knew I needed to protect my rights and, and proceed with legal action.

Q: Please describe the company's response to your requests stating that you were not entitled to commissions and there was no stock to anybody. Are you referring to Sonny Murphy's letter that he wrote in response to Exhibit 3 stating that position or was there some other communication? MR. WALLENDER: Objection to form.
A: I don't recall whether the decision was -- at what point in the process, the decision was made. It became clear at some point and I don't know at what point that was, after what specific conversation, it became clear that Sterling Planet's position was not mine, and that their -- they were not going to honor the terms of my employment contract.

Q: Prior to your termination, did Sterling Planet make you an offer to work as an independent contractor?
A: Yes.

Q: Were you not interested in accepting that offer? MR. WALLENDER: Object to form.
A: I did not want to leave the company. I did not want to lose my benefits. I did not want to lose my commissions, I did not want to lose the opportunity to earn commissions. So the answer is no, I did not want to become an independent consultant at will to the company with no guaranteed 40 hours and restrictive covenants. MR. COSTYN: Can we take a five-minute break real quick? MR. WALLENDER: Sure. (At this time a recess was taken.) MR. WALLENDER: During the break, I tried to find the exhibits you say were produced in discovery. I want to make clear again our request that you identify each of the Bates stamped pages. It's unclear to me and probably not correct that things that are attached as if they are put together in one exhibit were, in fact, attached, because I don't see them attached on these exhibits. For clarity, I would appreciate that. MR. COSTYN: Sure, and I apologize for not bringing stamped copies. MR. WALLENDER: And we will do the same for you. If we have exhibits, I will try to find the Bates stamped copies to use tomorrow. If not, I will provide them to you. MR. COSTYN: Sure. EXAMINATION BY MR. COSTYN:

Q: Back on the record, Ms. Bennett, if this lawsuit goes to trial, are there any witnesses you intend to call to support your case? MR. WALLENDER: I will object to the form. The decisions with respect to calling the witnesses are decisions of counsel, not decisions of Ms. Bennett. Are there any individuals that you are aware of that have firsthand knowledge of your claimed entitlement to commissions or stock? MR. WALLENDER: Object to form.
A: We have provided contact names of key Sterling Planet employees, and for sales contacts, for customer contacts.

Q: Are there any individuals who are not employees of Sterling Planet other than your attorney that you've discussed your lawsuit or your claims with? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: I have only discussed this with my attorney. I'm under a court order and a confidentiality agreement.

Q: Do you maintain communications with any former Sterling Planet employees?
A: Yes. MR. WALLENDER: Object to form.

Q: Which individuals that have been employed by Sterling Planet do you maintain contact with? MR. WALLENDER: Object to the form.
A: A number of them. Dell Jones, Greg Chambers I have seen at conferences, Marcus Krembs, Ron Mitchell, Joe Barclay. That may be all of the former employees.

Q: Have you maintained relationships or continuing relationships with current Sterling Planet employees? MR. WALLENDER: Object to form.
A: No.

Q: Have you filed for bankruptcy within the last five years?
A: I don't know whether it was in the last five years. I have. I have. I don't know whether it was in the last five years.

Q: Do you know the approximate date or just at some point?
A: Yes.

Q: Do you recall what court that was in?
A: Albany County.

Q: Was that bankruptcy filed under the name you provided at the beginning of this deposition?
A: Yes. MR. COSTYN: That's all the questions I have for you. EXAMINATION BY MR. WALLENDER:

Q: I have just a couple. I want to direct your attention to what was marked as Exhibit 2 in these proceedings. Can you find that document, please?
A: Yes.

Q: Do you have that document in front of you?
A: Yes. MR. WALLENDER: Mr. Costyn, do you have that copy? MR. COSTYN: I have it, yes.

Q: Do you recall being asked a question along the lines of whether Exhibit 2 referred to End-User Referral Forms?
A: I do, yes.

Q: Have you had a further opportunity to look at Exhibit 2?
A: I have.

Q: And does it, in fact, refer to End-User Referral Forms?
A: Yes.

Q: And can you explain how that is?
A: Under the detailed instructions for each lead entry section, under the fourth bold example, it talks about contact. It says, "Enter full contact information for each lead." This is the same information that was required for the End-User Referral Forms.

Q: Why does this document refer to End-User Referral Forms in the past tense?
A: Because Mel made the decision that we were replacing End-User Referral Forms with the Quickbase system.

Q: Do you recall being asked questions about your becoming responsible for the relationship with Intel Corporation?
A: Yes.

Q: And to your knowledge was your responsibility for that relationship communicated to Intel Corporation?
A: Yes.

Q: How was that done?
A: I had a conversation in Mel's office with Mel and Ron Mitchell and Joe Barclay, all on the phone with Marty Sedler, and it was communicated in the summer of '08 that, to Marty by Mel, that I was his account rep. And then, again, it was communicated directly to Marty with Paul Auger and me and Joe Barclay and Ron Mitchell and Mel Jones and others at a dinner at Elway's in Denver in October 2008.

Q: Who is Marty?
A: Marty Sedler is the VP for Energy. He is our point of contact, the decision-maker for the direct purchase at Intel.

Q: Who is Paul Auger?
A: Paul Auger is the global head of energy for PepsiCo.

Q: Was it ever indicated to Paul Auger you were the sales representative for the Pepsi relationship?
A: It was communicated to Paul at that same dinner at Elway's in Denver that I was his account rep from that point on.

Q: And who communicated that information at that dinner at John Elway's Restaurant?
A: Mel communicated that to him.

Q: What did Mel Jones say?
A: Mel said that I -- that they didn't have to deal with him any more, they got to deal with Kelly. We made jokes about how happy they were to be able to deal with me and not Mel. MR. WALLENDER: That's all I have at this juncture. MR. COSTYN: I've got no further questions.
